source_text:
Σοφίαν δὲ οὐ τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου οὐδὲ τῶν ἀρχόντων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου τῶν
καταργουμένων. Πρόεισι μὲν ὁ λόγος τῶν ἁγίων μυσταγωγῶν διὰ λέξεως χαμαιπετοῦς,
ἐνίησι δὲ τῶν θείων ἡμῖν μυστηρίων τὴν ἀκιβδήλευτον γνῶσιν, καὶ σοφίαν ὄντα
Χριστὸν ἀποφαίνει, οὐ διὰ τῆς τῶν ἐν κόσμῳ σοφῶν καλλιεπείας, ἀλλ' ἐξ ἰδίας φύσεως
μαρτυρούμενον, ὃν οὐδεὶς ἔγνω τῶν ἀρχόντων τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου, οἵ τινές εἰσιν αἱ
πονηραὶ δυνάμεις καὶ ἀντικείμεναι, αἵτινες λελαλήκασιν ἐν τοῖς τοῦ κόσμου σοφοῖς. Εἰ
γὰρ ἔγνωσαν, οὐκ ἂν τὸν Κύριον τῆς δόξης ἐσταύρωσαν. Ἔχει πολὺ τὸ εἰκὸς ὁ λόγος·
τεθριάμβευκε γὰρ ὁ Χριστὸς διὰ τοῦ ἰδίου σταυροῦ τὰς πονηρὰς καὶ ἀντικειμένας
δυνάμεις, προσηλώσας τῷ ξύλῳ "τὸ καθ' ἡμῶν χειρόγρα"φον," ἀπεσόβησεν τῆς καθ'
ἡμῶν τυραννίδος τὸν σατανᾶν, κατήργηκε τοῦ κόσμου τὴν ἁμαρτίαν, ἀνήκας τοῖς κάτω
πνεύμασι τὰς ᾅδου πύλας, καθεῖλε τοῦ θανάτου τὸ κράτος· εἶτα πῶς οὐκ ἀπηχθημένον
τοῖς ἀκαθάρτοις δαίμοσίν ἐστι τὸ ἐπὶ τῷ σταυρῷ πάθος; οὐκ ἂν οὖν ἐσταύρωσαν, εἴπερ
ᾔδεσαν ἀκριβῶς αὐτὸν ὄντα τὸν λυτρωτὴν καὶ τῆς δόξης Κύριον. ὅτι γὰρ διαβολικῆς
ἀγριότητος ἔργον ἦν τὸ διὰ τῆς ἰουδαίων ἀπονοίας σταυροῦσθαι Χριστὸν, παρέδειξεν
ἐναργῶς ὁ θεσπέσιος Ἰωάννης εἰπὼν περὶ τοῦ Ἰούδα "Μετὰ γὰρ τὸ "ψωμίον, φησὶν,
εἰσῆλθεν εἰς αὐτὸν ὁ σατανᾶς," ὃς οὐκ ᾔδει Θεὸν ὄντα τὸν Ἰησοῦν· εἰ γὰρ καὶ ἔγνω καὶ
ἐπέπειστο, πῶς ἐπείραζεν αὐτὸν ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ λέγων "Εἰ υἱὸς εἶ τοῦ 257 "Θεοῦ, εἰπὲ ἵνα
οἱ λίθοι οὗτοι ἄρτοι γένωνται;" γέγονε δὲ ὁμολογουμένως καὶ αὐτῷ τῷ Σωτῆρι σπουδὴ
τὸ λαθεῖν τοὺς ἄρχοντας τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου, ἵνα καὶ πάθοι λαθὼν καὶ τῷ ἰδίῳ αἵματι
κατακτήσηται τὴν ὑπ' οὐρανὸν ἑαυτῷ τε καὶ τῷ ἰδίῳ Πατρί. Καὶ τὰ βάθη τοῦ Θεοῦ. Βάθη
τοῦ Θεοῦ τῶν ἱερῶν γραμμάτων ἡ κεκρυμμένη καὶ ἀπόθετος γνῶσις, ἢν εἰδὸς τὸ
Πνεῦμα ταῖς τῶν ἁγίων ἀποκαλύπτει ψυχαῖς, θεῖόν τινα νοῦν ἀποφαῖνον τὸν ἐν αὐτοῖς.
Ψυχικὸς δὲ ἄνθρωπος. Ψυχικός ἐστιν ὁ κατὰ σάρκα ζῶν καὶ μήπω τὸν νοῦν φωτισθεὶς
διὰ τοῦ Πνεύματος, ἀλλὰ μόνην τὴν ἔμφυτον καὶ ἀνθρωπίνην σύνεσιν ἔχων, ἣν ταῖς
ἁπάντων ψυχαῖς ἐμβάλλει ὁ δημιουργός. Ὁ δὲ πνευματικὸς ἀνακρίνει μὲν πάντα. Ὁ
πνευματικὸς ἀνακρίνει μὲν πάντα καὶ οἷον καταλεπτύνει ταῖς ἀκριβείαις, ἀνακρίνεται
δὲ ὑπ' οὐδενὸς αὐτός· ὅτι δὲ τοῖς λεγομένοις εἶναι ψυχικοῖς δεῖ δὴ πάντως εἰς ὄνησιν
καὶ παιδαγωγίαν πνευματικῶν διδασκάλων, καθίστησιν ἐναργὲς προστιθείς τε καὶ
λέγων Τίς γὰρ ἔγνω νοῦν Κυρίου ὃς συμβιβάσει αὐτόν; ὅμοιον ὡσεὶ λέγοι Τὸν ψυχικὸν
ἄνθρωπον συμβιβάσειεν ἂν οὐδεὶς, εἰ μὴ νοῦν ἔχοι Χριστοῦ· τὸ δὲ 258 συμβιβάσαι φησὶν
ἀντὶ τοῦ νοῆσαι παρασκευάσει· καὶ τίνες ἂν εἶεν οἱ νοῦν ἔχοντες Κυρίου, πάλιν αὐτὸς
παρέδειξεν εἰπών Ἡμεῖς δὲ νοῦν Χριστοῦ ἔχομεν, τουτέστι τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ λαλοῦν ἐν
ἁγίοις, καὶ ἐκκαλύπτον αὐτοῖς μυστήρια, καὶ θεῖόν τινα νοῦν ἀποφαῖνον τὸν ἐν αὐτοῖς.
οὐκοῦν ὧν γεγράφασι τὰ ἀμείνω τε καὶ ὑψηλότερα, νοεῖν τε καὶ λέγειν δυναμένοις
συμμεμετρήκασιν οἰκονομικῶς ταῖς τῶν μυσταγωγουμένων ἕξεσι τὴν ὑφήγησιν. Καὶ
ἐγὼ, ἀδελφοὶ, οὐκ ἠδυνήθην λαλῆσαι ὑμῖν ὡς πνευματικοῖς, ἀλλ' ὡς σαρκικοῖς, ὡς
νηπίοις ἐν Χριστῷ. Οὐχ ὡς ἀπορῶν τοῦ λόγου πρὸς τελείαν γνῶσιν ἀνακομίζειν
ἰσχύοντος ἐκωλύθην ὑμῖν λαλῆσαι τὰ τελειότερα, ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ νήπιοί ἐστε τὴν ἕξιν καὶ
ἀνασφαλῆ τὸν νοῦν ἔχετε, μὴ προβεβηκότα πρὸς εἴδησιν τῶν τελειωτέρων, καὶ οὐ
δυνάμενον χωρεῖν τέως μυστήρια. Ἐγὼ ἐφύτευσα. Ἐφύτευσε μὲν Παῦλος, ὁ δὲ Ἀπολλὼς
ἐπότισεν, ἐκάλει πρὸς αὔξησιν Θεός. τίς οὖν ἡ φύτευσις ἢ τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ τῆς πίστεως, καὶ
ὅτι τῶν ὅλων Κύριος ὁ Θεὸς ἐπιγνῶναί τε καὶ εἰπεῖν; τίς δὲ ὁ ποτισμὸς ἢ τῶν ἐκ
διδασκαλίας λόγων οἱονεὶ καταβολὴ καὶ ἐπίχυσις, τρέφουσα πρὸς εὐρωστίαν τὸν τοῦ
pass_a_gloss: Wisdom (σοφίαν) but not of the age (αἰῶνος) this nor of the rulers (ἀρχόντων) of this age, the ones being abolished (καταργουμένων). Goes forth (πρόεισι) the word of the holy initiators (μυσταγωγῶν) through diction ground-falling (χαμαιπετοῦς), but sends into (ἐνίησι) us of the divine mysteries (μυστηρίων) the unadulterated (ἀκιβδήλευτον) knowledge (γνῶσιν), and shows forth (ἀποφαίνει) Christ being wisdom, not through the fine-speech (καλλιεπείας) of the wise in the world, but from own nature (φύσεως) being witnessed (μαρτυρούμενον), whom none knew of the rulers of this age, who are the wicked and opposing powers (δυνάμεις ἀντικείμεναι), which have spoken in the wise of the world. For if they had known, not would they the Lord of glory (Κύριον τῆς δόξης) have crucified (ἐσταύρωσαν). Has much likelihood (εἰκός) the word; for has triumphed (τεθριάμβευκε) Christ through own cross (σταυροῦ) the wicked and opposing powers, having nailed (προσηλώσας) to the wood (ξύλῳ) 'the against-us handwriting (χειρόγραφον)', scared off (ἀπεσόβησεν) from the against-us tyranny (τυραννίδος) Satan, abolished (κατήργηκε) of the world the sin, opened/let open (ἀνήκας) to the spirits below the gates of Hades (ᾅδου πύλας), pulled down (καθεῖλε) of death the might (κράτος); then how not hateful (ἀπηχθημένον) to the unclean demons is the on-the-cross suffering (πάθος)? Not then would they have crucified, if they had known exactly him being the redeemer (λυτρωτήν) and of glory Lord. That for of devilish savagery (διαβολικῆς ἀγριότητος) work was the through the Jews' madness (ἀπονοίας) being crucified Christ, showed clearly the divine (θεσπέσιος) John saying about Judas 'For after the morsel (ψωμίον), he says, entered into him Satan', who did not know God being Jesus; for if indeed he knew and was persuaded (ἐπέπειστο), how was he tempting (ἐπείραζεν) him in the desert saying 'If son you are of God, say that these stones become loaves'? Came to be admittedly (ὁμολογουμένως) also to the Saviour himself an eagerness (σπουδή) the escaping notice (λαθεῖν) of the rulers of this age, so that also he might suffer unnoticed and by own blood (αἵματι) acquire (κατακτήσηται) the under-heaven for himself and for own Father. And the depths (βάθη) of God. Depths of God: of the sacred letters (ἱερῶν γραμμάτων) the hidden (κεκρυμμένη) and stored-away (ἀπόθετος) knowledge, which knowing the Spirit (Πνεῦμα) to the souls of the saints reveals (ἀποκαλύπτει), a divine mind (θεῖον νοῦν) showing (ἀποφαῖνον) the one in them. Natural (ψυχικός) but man. Natural is the one according to flesh (κατὰ σάρκα) living and not yet in mind enlightened (φωτισθείς) through the Spirit, but only the inborn (ἔμφυτον) and human understanding (σύνεσιν) having, which into the souls of all casts the craftsman (δημιουργός). The spiritual (πνευματικός) but examines (ἀνακρίνει) all. The spiritual examines all and as it were thins-down (καταλεπτύνει) by exactnesses, is examined but by none himself; that to the ones said to be natural there is need by all means for benefit (ὄνησιν) and child-training (παιδαγωγίαν) of spiritual teachers, he establishes clear adding and saying 'For who knew mind of Lord who will instruct (συμβιβάσει) him?'; like as if he said 'The natural man no one would instruct, unless he had mind of Christ'; the 'instruct' he says instead of 'will prepare to understand (νοῆσαι)'; and who would be the ones having mind of Lord, again he himself showed saying 'We but mind of Christ have', that is the Spirit speaking in saints, and uncovering (ἐκκαλύπτον) to them mysteries, and a divine mind showing the one in them. Therefore of what they have written the better and higher, to [ones] able both to understand and to speak, they have measured together (συμμεμετρήκασιν) economically (οἰκονομικῶς) to the states (ἕξεσι) of the ones being initiated (μυσταγωγουμένων) the guidance (ὑφήγησιν). And I, brothers, was not able to speak to you as to spiritual, but as to fleshly (σαρκικοῖς), as to infants (νηπίοις) in Christ. Not as lacking the word able to carry up to perfect knowledge was I hindered (ἐκωλύθην) to speak to you the more perfect things, but since infants you are in state (ἕξιν) and unsteady (ἀνασφαλῆ) the mind have, not having advanced to knowledge of the more perfect, and not able to contain (χωρεῖν) yet mysteries. I planted (ἐφύτευσα). Planted Paul, but Apollos watered (ἐπότισεν), was calling to growth (αὔξησιν) God. What then the planting (φύτευσις) or the [thing] in beginning of faith (πίστεως), and that of all Lord [is] God to recognise (ἐπιγνῶναι) and to say? What but the watering (ποτισμός) or of the from-teaching (διδασκαλίας) words as it were a sowing-down (καταβολή) and pouring-on (ἐπίχυσις), nourishing (τρέφουσα) to robustness (εὐρωστίαν) the [mind] of the one who believed, so that it might appear also fruit-bearing (καρποφόρος)? [last clause from head of u02-open]
pass_b_english: “Yet a wisdom not of this age, nor of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing” (1 Corinthians 2:6). The word of the holy teachers of the mysteries goes forth in lowly speech, yet it plants in us an unadulterated knowledge of the divine mysteries. It shows that Christ is wisdom, not through the fine speech of the world’s wise men, but as he is attested by his own nature. None of the rulers of this age knew him (1 Corinthians 2:8). These rulers are the evil and hostile powers, who have spoken through the wise men of the world.

“For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). The saying is very reasonable. For by his own cross Christ triumphed over the evil and hostile powers, nailing to the wood “the bond written against us” (Colossians 2:14–15). He drove Satan away from his tyranny over us, abolished the sin of the world, opened the gates of Hades to the spirits below, and pulled down the power of death. How, then, could the suffering on the cross be anything but hateful to the unclean demons? So they would not have crucified him, had they known for certain that he was the Redeemer and the Lord of glory.

That the crucifixion of Christ, carried out through the madness of the Jews, was the work of the devil’s savagery, the inspired John showed plainly when he said of Judas, “After the morsel, Satan entered into him” (John 13:27). Satan did not know that Jesus was God. For if he had known and been convinced of it, how could he have tempted him in the desert, saying, “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew 4:3)? And the Savior himself, as all agree, took care to escape the notice of the rulers of this age, so that, unnoticed, he might suffer, and by his own blood win for himself and for his own Father all that lies under heaven.

“Even the depths of God” (1 Corinthians 2:10). The depths of God are the hidden knowledge laid up in the sacred writings. The Spirit knows it and reveals it to the souls of the saints, and makes the mind within them a divine mind.

“The natural man” (1 Corinthians 2:14). The natural man is the one who lives according to the flesh and has not yet had his mind enlightened through the Spirit. He has only the inborn, human understanding which the Creator puts into the souls of all.

“But the spiritual man judges all things” (1 Corinthians 2:15). The spiritual man judges all things and, so to speak, sifts them finely with exact care, but he himself is judged by no one. That those called natural need spiritual teachers, by all means, for their benefit and training, Paul makes plain by adding, “For who has known the mind of the Lord, so as to instruct him?” (1 Corinthians 2:16; Isaiah 40:13). It is as if he said: No one could instruct the natural man unless he had the mind of Christ. By “instruct” he means “prepare him to understand.” And who are those that have the mind of the Lord? He showed this himself when he went on, “But we have the mind of Christ” (1 Corinthians 2:16), that is, the Spirit who speaks in the saints, unveils mysteries to them, and makes the mind within them a divine mind.

So, although the saints could have understood and spoken things better and loftier than what they wrote, they wisely measured their teaching to the state of those they were leading into the mysteries.

“And I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spiritual men, but as to men of the flesh, as to infants in Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:1). It was not for want of a word strong enough to raise you to perfect knowledge that I was kept from speaking to you of the more perfect things. It was because you are infants in your condition and have an unsteady mind, one that has not yet advanced to the knowledge of the more perfect things and cannot yet take in mysteries.

“I planted” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Paul planted, Apollos watered, and God called them to growth. What, then, is the planting, if not what belongs to the beginning of faith: to acknowledge and to say that God is the Lord of all? And what is the watering, if not the sowing and pouring in, as it were, of the words that come from teaching, which nourish the believer’s mind to strength so that it may also prove fruitful?

choices.why: Traditional rendering; follows Cyril's own definition.
Colossians 2:14; the sense is a written record of debt.
In Cyril's reading the object is the natural man, not the Lord.
The context is a wavering mind.

Critical: in Cyril's reading of 1 Corinthians 2:16 the object αὐτόν is the natural man ('no one could instruct the natural man unless he had the mind of Christ'), so the quotation must read 'instruct him', not 'instruct Him'. Wrong sense: ὧν γεγράφασι τὰ ἀμείνω τε καὶ ὑψηλότερα is a genitive of comparison: the saints could have said things better and loftier than what they wrote, not 'the better part of what they wrote'. The lemma's verb ἀνακρίνει is kept as 'judges ... is judged' in the comment as in the lemma, not switched to 'examines'. Ἔχει πολὺ τὸ εἰκός is 'very reasonable', not 'entirely'. 'he says' was added with no φησί in the Greek; removed. εἰπεῖν is 'say', not 'confess'. Pronouns for Christ lowercased and 'Saviour'/'recognise' spelled 'Savior'/'acknowledge' to match u01-rem-early/mid and the book's existing rows (lowercase pronouns, American spelling).
